title: Transversus abdominis plane block vs. rectus sheath catheter for postoperative pain management following abdominal surgery
summary:
Pain in the abdominal wall often occurs after abdominal surgery because many pain-sensitive nerves run through that area. Local therapy (administered directly at the surgical site) is preferred for treating this pain because it targets the specific area and causes fewer side effects than treatment that affects the entire body.
The study compares two established procedures:
1. A single dose of a pain reliever administered into the abdominal wall during surgery
2. continuous administration of a painkiller via a catheter after surgery
During surgery, a pain catheter is placed on both sides of the incision site. Depending on random assignment, the patient will either receive pain medication through this catheter or a painkiller depot will be administered directly during surgery (the catheter then contains only saline solution). Both methods are effective; the aim of the study is to determine which is superior.
After surgery, pain is assessed regularly. If necessary, the patient receives additional pain medication. The catheter is usually removed on the 3rd day after surgery. Participation in the study ends upon discharge from the hospital.

interventions.name:
Placement of a posterior transversus abdominis plane block at the end of abdominal surgery infiltrating ropivacaine
Placement of a rectus sheath catheter at the end of abdominal surgery and infusion of a placebo for 3 days postoperatively

Placement of a posterior transversus abdominis plane block at the end of abdominal surgery infiltrating a placebo
Placement of a rectus sheath catheter at the end of abdominal surgery and infusion of ropivacaine for 3 days postoperatively

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
●     Elective laparoscopic, robot-assisted, or open abdominal surgery of the lower gastrointestinal tract or sarcoma surgery
●     Open surgical procedures involving a median laparotomy
●     Capacity to consent
●     ASA 1–3
●     ECOG 0–2
Exclusion criteria:
●   Abdominoperineal resection
●     Open surgical procedures using an approach other than median laparotomy (transverse laparotomy, costal margin incision, pararectal incision, etc.)
●     Opiates as part of long-term medication
●     Pre-existing chronic abdominal pain
●     Extensive previous surgery with scarring of the abdominal wall
●     Post-abdominal wall reconstruction
●      Allergy to local anesthetics or opioids
●     End-stage renal failure (<30 ml/min)
●     Severe liver disease
●     Metastatic disease
●     Pre-existing hematological disease or coagulation disorder
●     Pregnancy
